blocks.text: Picture one of the loudest men in American business. Now picture him as a small boy in suburban Detroit, standing outside Hebrew school and struggling to breathe. Steve Ballmer was so shy as a child that going to class made him hyperventilate. His mother had to talk him through it.
I was just so scared. So I wouldn't throw up, my mom would have to make me take short breaths.
blocks.who: Steve Ballmer, on going to Hebrew school as a boy

blocks.text: This is the man who later screamed "developers" on stage. Remember this boy.
A translator and a junk dealer's daughter

Steven Anthony Ballmer was born in Detroit on ==24 March 1956==. The family lived first in Oak Park and then in Farmington Hills, two suburbs of the city that built America's cars. One old family photo printed by the Detroit Jewish News shows him as a little boy in Oak Park, in his firetruck in the neighborhood. That picture is about all the public record offers of Steve at five.

His father was born Fritz Hans Ballmer in Switzerland and became Frederic Henry in America. People called him Fred. Fred had one huge talent: he spoke six languages. After the Second World War, while still in his twenties, that talent put him inside one of the most serious rooms on earth. He worked as an interpreter at the Nuremberg trials and at the war crimes trials in Dachau.

Those languages also got Fred a job and a chance to move to the United States. But America did not hand him anything. Steve has described his father moving from job to job: hotel lobby receptionist, payroll clerk, assembly-line worker. Only after that did he reach a mid-level job at the Ford Motor Company. __The man who had interpreted at Nuremberg started again near the bottom, and kept climbing.__
Six languages. Nuremberg. Then a hotel front desk. Immigrant life in one line.

Steve's mother, Beatrice Dworkin, was called Bea. She was a Detroit girl, and Steve says she was born on 12th Street. Her father, Sam, was a Jewish immigrant who had been a cobbler in Russia. The family story, told in the Detroit Jewish News, is that he came from Belarus and avoided persecution as a Jew in the tsar's army. In Detroit he started in junk and came to own an auto parts shop.

So this was a car family on both sides, one at the big company and one at the small shop. Steve's grandfather lived at Wabash and Grand River, then moved to McNichols near Greenfield. His cousins grew up on Outer Drive. When Steve talks about Detroit today, those neighborhoods are what he means, not the fancy downtown. His mother was also a first cousin of the mother of the comic Gilda Radner, which made Steve and Radner second cousins.

items.label: the family lived in Belgium for Ford

blocks.text: Not rich, and never told otherwise

Steve has a short summary of the money situation: he grew up middle-class. Fred's job at Ford was mid-level, not a seat in the boardroom. A review of the 2002 biography Bad Boy Ballmer puts it sharply. Many Ford managers' families lived in the smart suburb of Birmingham, and the Ballmers could not afford to. There was also a sister, Shelley.

Neither parent had been to college. Steve says his father did not even finish high school. Yet Fred loved working through hard details. Steve remembers him explaining the tax rules on a special kind of export company, seeing every angle, and he says he could never follow how his father did it. The lesson of that house was simple: you don't need a degree to think hard, but you should get one anyway.

Faith in the home was mixed too. Fred was a Swiss Protestant and Bea was Jewish, and Steve still calls himself an ethnic Jew rather than a religious one. His mother studied Hebrew alongside him. Stories of Jewish persecution were common talk when he was growing up. Decades later, in 2015, he studied for a year and a half and finally had his bar mitzvah, at a temple in Bellevue, Washington.
A bar mitzvah in his late fifties. Never too late to finish something.
The year he turned eight

Two things happened around age eight that shaped everything after. First, Fred told his son he was going to Harvard. This was a father who had never been to college, and he kept saying it. Growing up in Europe, Steve later explained, Harvard was the one American school you had heard of.

Second, Ford sent Fred overseas because he spoke so many languages. The family moved to Brussels and stayed three years. Steve has called it "kind of a nutty thing" for the time. There was very little English on TV, and Europe was still coming out of the war. He described it as being in an isolation chamber, but he also says it gave him a global view. A book summary says he came out speaking perfect French.

They arrived in May, while he was in second grade, so he had about a month at an international school before summer. The teacher then told his parents something no parent wants to hear. Steve was bad at math, the teacher said, and might struggle in third grade because of it. Yes, that Steve Ballmer. The boy who would one day outscore Bill Gates in a national math contest was told he was weak at math.
I call that motivating.
blocks.who: Steve Ballmer, on the teacher who said he was bad at math

blocks.text: For example: he spent the whole summer between second and third grade studying math because he did not want to fail. It worked so well that he lasted three weeks in third grade. Then the school moved him up to fourth.
Read this twice. Bad at math in May. Skipped a grade by fall.

__Fear of falling behind became his engine, and that pattern would repeat.__ In sixth grade he took what he now calls the most important math class of his life. There were two math classes that year: a regular one, and one called mental math, where you worked only with numbers in your head. He says it made him comfortable with numbers. Later at Microsoft, staff would joke that a meeting with him was like going to math camp.
Coming home to a city on fire

The family came back to Michigan in ==1967==, when Steve was about 11. The Detroit Jewish News records that his hometown was in flames that year. In the early hours of 23 July, police raided an unlicensed bar at 12th Street and Clairmount. What followed lasted five days and brought in the National Guard and the US Army. The toll was 43 dead, nearly 1,700 fires and more than 7,000 arrests.

photo.caption: Michigan National Guard troops during the Detroit uprising, 24 July 1967. The Ballmers came home to this city that year.
photo.author: 岩波書店

blocks.text: 12th Street is the street where, Steve says, his mother was born. He still talks about Detroit through its neighborhoods, and today he and his wife Connie fund anti-poverty work in the city. When people say Detroit has come back, he rolls his eyes. He tells them to drive up Grand River from Detroit to Farmington Hills and see what work is left to do.

items.text: Born in Detroit on 24 March. Grows up in Oak Park, then Farmington Hills.
His father tells him he is headed for Harvard.
Ford sends the family to Brussels. A teacher says he is bad at math.
Studies math all summer and is moved from third grade up to fourth.
Takes "mental math", the class he later calls the most important of his life.
The family returns to Michigan in the year of the Detroit uprising.

blocks.text: So look at what this quiet kid had by age 12. He had an immigrant father with no degree and a very big plan. He had a mother who would calm him down, and who would soon be driving him around Michigan. He had lived on another continent. And he had one private discovery: being told you are behind can be the best thing that ever happens to you, if you answer it with work.

After eighth grade, Steve won a scholarship to Detroit Country Day School, a demanding private school in Beverly Hills, Michigan. It should have been a triumph. Then he walked in and found out that everyone else had already done a year of algebra. He had not. He had come from a public school that moved more slowly, and he was a full year behind.
Scholarship kid. Behind on day one. Have you felt this? So did he.

He says he got scared, and then he got motivated. It was the Brussels feeling all over again. In March of that first year, a math teacher made him an offer. If he wanted, they could do algebra two while still finishing algebra one, and he would catch up with the rest of the class. He took it.

The teacher Steve credits by name is Edward Kuss, whom he calls "a major force in my life" for lighting up his interest in math. Kuss later became an actuary in Ohio. He remembered Steve as a joy to teach because "he just soaked it up." After ninth grade, Steve also went off to a math camp, and he joined a summer National Science Foundation program for advanced students.
He came here in the ninth grade, and he was probably a year or two behind us in math. By the end of the tenth grade, he was a year and a half ahead of us.
blocks.who: Todd Rich, Country Day classmate, in Bad Boy Ballmer

blocks.text: __A single teacher who offers a harder path can change a whole life.__ Notice what the teacher did not do. He did not give Steve an easier version of the class. He offered more work, and he trusted the kid to want it. If you are ever behind, go and look for that teacher, and say yes when they offer.
The kid with chalk in one hand

Classmates and teachers talked to biographer Fredric Maxwell for his 2002 book, and their memories match. Steve sat in the front row with his hand up. He would not rest until he understood a thing. The school uniform was only required one day a week, and he wore it every day anyway. One classmate's word for him was "hardcore", a word Steve himself would later use as the highest praise.

For example: his math teacher Gerald Hansen remembered Steve at the blackboard, explaining a problem with his hands flying. He would write with one hand and hold an eraser in the other, writing and erasing at the same time. Hansen called it intellectual energy, and said you could never stump him.

Here is the strange part. Inside, he says, he was still a very, very shy person who had a hard time speaking up in class. Both things seem to have been true at once. The energy poured out at the blackboard, where he was sure of the answer. The nerves stayed for everything else.
Shy people can still be intense. You don't have to pick one.
College math at night, age 16

By his junior and senior years, the school had run out of math to give him. So Steve started taking college math at night and co-enrolled at Lawrence Institute of Technology, now Lawrence Technological University. He also attended its Summer Science Institute after junior year. Taking a high school student was rare for them, and an administrator there arranged it specially. Steve went on to earn an A in each of the college's six hardest math classes.
It was not unheard of, but it was unusual for us at the time to accept a student still in high school.
blocks.who: Richard Marburger, then a dean and later president of Lawrence Tech

blocks.text: His mother became his driver, taking him to math contests all over Michigan. It paid off. In the Michigan Mathematics Prize Competition he won Gold and Silver Awards in his final two years of school, and one account places him in the top 10 in the state. Now the wow detail: another teenager in the same contest, from North Farmington High School, placed in the top 50 as a senior. His name was Bill Joy, and he would go on to co-found Sun Microsystems.

That same patch of suburban Detroit also produced Scott McNealy, later the CEO of Sun. McNealy was a crosstown friend of Steve's, and the two later shared a room on a recruiting trip to Harvard. Years afterward they fought loudly in public as business rivals, and McNealy joked about "Ballmer and Butthead." So one set of Detroit suburbs gave computing three of its biggest names, in the shadow of the car factories.
Your rival might be the kid across town right now.
The sport he was bad at

Steve loved basketball and was not good at it. His highest level of play, he admits, was ninth grade, on a team that cut nobody. On the track team he threw the shot put. What impressed Edward Kuss most was something else. The math star said his proudest achievement was shaving ==20 seconds== off his time in the quarter-mile, and even then the time wasn't good.
But the things he had to struggle with were the things that gave him the most satisfaction.

If he couldn't star on the basketball team, he would run it. He became team manager and took the job as seriously as a final exam. He was a perfectionist with the statistics. He made sure the towels and balls were in order and that water bottles were ready when players came off the court. "And, of course, he cheered," his coach told Maxwell.

In pick-up games he never stopped trying. A childhood friend, Rob Mason, remembered him being so loud as he called out to see who wanted to play. "He just kept driving toward the basket," Mason said. "He was hugely competitive." Decades later, when a radio host called him an athlete, Steve set the record straight: "I was a big guy, a team manager and a math major."
Water-bottle boy. Now he owns an NBA team. Do the small job well.
What he did not do

Founder stories love a teenage hustle, so here is an honest report. We looked for a Ballmer first business, a teen deal, a side income, and we could not find one in any reliable source. Compare Bill Gates, who was already earning money writing code with friends in high school. Steve joined things instead. He was president of the school's political club and its computer club, on top of math and sport.

__You do not need a startup at 16 to matter later.__ What he built as a teenager was not a company. He built the habit of being behind, panicking, working absurdly hard, and passing everyone. He also learned he enjoyed serving a team from the sideline. Neither one shows up on a resume, but both ran his entire career.

blocks.text: The legend gets corrected

Almost every profile of Steve Ballmer says he got a perfect 800 on the math SAT. The New York Times said it, Business Week said it, and his Harvard paper once said he got a perfect 1600. In 2019 the interviewer David Rubenstein said it to his face on stage. Steve stopped him at once.
Seven-ninety, not 800. This is the facts. And numbers describe these things very well.
He corrected a compliment. On stage. That is respect for numbers.

He finished as valedictorian of his class and a National Merit Scholar. He applied to Harvard, Caltech and MIT, and got into all three, which he jokes proves his numbers orientation. Then he did what his father had been announcing since he was eight. He chose Harvard, and became the first in his family to go to college.

items.text: Wins a scholarship to Detroit Country Day School.
Arrives a year behind in math. Doubles up on algebra from March, then goes to math camp.
By a classmate's memory, he is now a year and a half ahead.
Takes college math at Lawrence Tech and wins state math prizes.
Graduates as valedictorian at 17 and heads to Harvard.

blocks.text: He left for Massachusetts in 1973 with his whole future worked out. He was "hell bent and determined", as he puts it, to get a PhD in either math or physics. The only question was which one. A classmate guessed that twenty years on he would be designing computer chips. Everyone who knew him was sure of the same broad thing: this boy was going to be a scientist. Everyone was wrong.

chapters.title: Too Bad You Don't Have a Twin

blocks.text: Steve arrived at Harvard in 1973 and tried to sign up for both Math 55 and Physics 55 at once. A kindly adviser stopped him. "Young Steve, big mistake," he recalls being told. So he took one and did an independent study in the other. He also did something odd for a shy kid. He memorized the names and faces of his classmates from the class registry.
Very useful trick for shy people: learn the names first.
A score of 33

His first exam was in physics. He walked out and called his parents. "I think I just flunked out of school," he told them. He was already doing statistics for the Harvard football team and was meant to travel to the game at Penn. He stayed behind, crushed, and went to see his adviser.

The next week the paper came back. He had scored ==33 out of 100==. Then he learned that the median was 25, and that 33 put him about fifth or sixth in the class. So he had not failed at all. But one student had scored far higher than everyone else, and that student went on to be a physics professor. Steve looked at that score and drew a conclusion that changed his life.
So it took me about two months to learn I wasn't a physicist and I wasn't a genius.

He says everything good started right there. He also noticed something about how he felt on those long evenings of problem sets. He was alone in his room, and after about three hours he just could not take any more. The most hardcore math students could power through anything. "By the end of my freshman year, I decided it wasn't me," he told the New York Times. "I knew I needed more interaction with people for me to be happy."

__Knowing what you are not is worth as much as knowing what you are.__ Plenty of bright students spend ten years chasing the career everyone expected of them. Steve dropped his by the end of his first year, while still keeping math as part of his degree. He switched to applied math and economics. He was not leaving the numbers. He was leaving the empty room.
He was 18, and he dropped the plan everyone expected of him.
Majoring in extracurriculars

After that he threw himself at campus life. He has said it sounds like he majored in extracurriculars, and that this is actually true. At one point he was manager of the football team, publisher of the literary magazine The Advocate and advertising manager of The Crimson, all at the same time. He was also in the Hasty Pudding and Fox clubs. And he taught a pre-calculus course, Math A, which forced him to explain ideas simply.

The earliest pay we can find for him came here. He kept track of rebounds and assists at Harvard basketball games for ==$12 a game==, which he says he would have attended for free. He admits he gave one player, Lou Silver, the benefit of the doubt on every rebound. When Steve bought the LA Clippers roughly four decades later, Silver was one of the first people to email him.

For example: to win a place on The Crimson's business side, he had to go out and sell $1,000 of advertising, which felt like a lot of money. Then he took on ad sales. The Crimson's business manager remembered him bursting through the front door and yelling that he had closed an account.

Selling ads taught him something no exam could. Grades only measure you, he says, but a small paper with no money needs real revenue. He calls this owning the results. At The Advocate, fellow staffer Peter Alson called him "the perfect publisher" and added, "He was great with money." Another Crimson colleague remembered him filling the entrance so you had to squeeze past him, and said it was quite hard to dislike him.

The football job did something bigger still. A manager at Harvard was not a respected position. But at every team meal he had to stand up, shout "listen up" and make the coaches' announcements to the whole team. He calls it a transformative experience for a boy who had been very shy. __The lowest job on the team became his public-speaking school.__
Very important for first-time founders! Pick the job that scares you.

There was a price. He says he attended "all of one class session" in senior year, and that junior year was only a little better. Taking on The Advocate was the job that broke the bank, forcing him to learn to manage his time. That lesson stuck. For years at Microsoft he kept spreadsheets comparing the hours he had budgeted with the hours he actually spent.
Down the hall from Bill

In sophomore year Steve lived in Currier House, an out-of-the-way dorm full of math and science students. A fellow sophomore named Bill Gates lived down the same hall. A dorm mate, Jeff Clark, introduced them. On the surface they had nothing in common, and Gates has a perfect line about why they were friends with the same guy.
Jeff liked Steve because Steve had this very energetic approach to being involved in everything. And he kind of liked me because I had this very energetic approach to not being involved in things.

photo.caption: Currier House at Harvard, where Steve Ballmer and Bill Gates lived down the hall from each other.
photo.author: Daderot

blocks.text: What joined them was intensity. They would argue and study at high volume, both rocking back and forth. They went to a double bill of Singin' in the Rain and A Clockwork Orange, two films linked by one song, and their own version of that song back at Currier set off a heated exchange with a dorm mate. Gates's own verdict was that they then became "super-good friends." Steve, the social one, later got his friend into the Fox Club through a ritual of tipsy hazing and storytelling.

They also took a tough graduate economics class together and barely went to the lectures. Then came one week of late-night cramming, with Steve swinging between screams of "we're golden" and "no, we're not." Gates got the top grade and Steve the second. On the Putnam, the top math contest for college students in the US and Canada, the order flipped. "I was 57th in the nation and Bill was, I think, 97th or something," Steve says. Asked if he ever mentions it to Gates: "Not of late, no."

photo.caption: The Poker Room at Currier House, where all-night card games ran in Gates's time at Harvard. Photographed in 2012.
photo.author: Tbuckley89

blocks.text: Then Gates was gone. In early 1975 he and Paul Allen threw themselves into writing software for a new home computer, and that summer Gates left Cambridge for New Mexico. Steve stayed and finished. He graduated magna cum laude in applied math and economics in 1977. But they stayed close. "I was his business buddy," Steve told the Detroit News. "When Bill needed a business person versus a technical person, he'd give me a call."
Brownie mix, Cincinnati

Stanford's business school accepted him, but he put it off to get some real experience first. After a visit to see Gates in Albuquerque, he chose between two jobs. One was with a then-small car insurer in Cleveland, Progressive. The other was at Procter & Gamble, which had the best training for young business people at the time. He picked Procter & Gamble in Cincinnati.

He was still terrified. A colleague who became his friend and roommate remembered their first meeting well, and Steve still repeats it to interviewers. It went like this: "Hi, my name's Steve Ballmer. My-- my palms are sweating but don't worry, I'm OK." That is the future CEO of Microsoft on his first day at work, at 21.

The work was as unglamorous as it sounds. He was an assistant product manager working on Duncan Hines brownie mix, blueberry muffin mix and Moist 'n' Easy Snack Cake. He also sold a gadget called the Coldsnap Freezer Dessert Maker, and thirty years later he could still recite its slogan: "Makes revolutionary desserts you never could have thought of before." Part of his job involved redesigning food-mix boxes.
Every great career has a brownie mix chapter. Don't be embarrassed by yours.

He shared his cubicle with a 22-year-old Dartmouth graduate named Jeff Immelt. Fortune described the pair in mid-1978, rewriting memos and playing waste-bin basketball with the wadded-up paper. Business Week's version has them playing Nerf basketball. Neither had a career plan. One of them later recalled: "We were voted the two guys probably least likely to succeed."

Before they turned 50, those two would be running Microsoft and General Electric. __Nobody can read your future from your first job, including your first boss.__ Steve still rates what the place taught him, and he points out that Meg Whitman and Steve Case came through Procter & Gamble around then too. What he missed was the people. He wanted to work for really smart people, and he says he did not find that everywhere there.
The Hollywood detour

Here is a part of the story many people never hear. In the spring of 1979 this Harvard math graduate moved to Los Angeles to try the movie business. It did not go well. He ended up reading B-movie scripts for NBC and parking cars at charity auctions. He decided that a safer bet was Stanford after all.
Future CEO, parking cars at 23. Failed experiments are cheap at this age.
Stanford, and the classmate from India

He enrolled at Stanford's Graduate School of Business in the fall of 1979, having paid his first visit to Seattle that summer to see Gates. He loved the first year. Two consulting firms each offered a ==$10,000== prize for the most promising first-year student, and he won both. Indian readers will enjoy one more detail about that class. "Mukesh was my class at Stanford," Steve said in a 2008 speech. "He and I both dropped out." He meant Mukesh Ambani, who went home to help his father with the family textile business.

photo.caption: Stanford's business school as it looks today, seen from Encina Hall. Ballmer and Mukesh Ambani were in the same class here.
photo.author: Effeietsanders

blocks.text: By spring 1980 he was hunting for a summer job. He had four good ideas: a consulting firm, Morgan Stanley, Progressive Insurance, or Ford, his father's company. He even had a spring break trip lined up to visit them, including McKinsey in Chicago and Bain and BCG in Boston. Then the phone rang. It was Bill.
Hey, too bad you don't have a twin brother. We could kind of use somebody like you around here now.
blocks.who: Bill Gates, recruiting Steve Ballmer by phone, as Ballmer retold it in 2007

blocks.text: That was the entire pitch. Steve thought about it for a day. He knew almost nothing about the business. He had written a few programs for a modeling class, and he knew Microsoft led the world in something new. But Bill was the smartest person he had ever met, and he wanted to work for smart people. So he cut his trip short and flew to Seattle.
Read this twice. He chose the person, not the industry.

Gates had a standard recruiting trick then: he got his parents to work you over. His father was 6 foot 7 and hard to say no to. Gates then left for his first vacation and left Steve alone in his house, telling him to enjoy it and try to lock the door on his way out. The two made a deal. If it did not work out by the end of summer, either one could end it with no hard feelings, and Steve could go back to Stanford.
The toughest call

Stanford agreed to hold his place, while asking whether this was really a wise decision. Then he had to phone home. His father had carried this Harvard dream for years, and had already worried that Stanford was too obscure a choice. Now his son was leaving it for "some fly-by-night outfit in Seattle run by a buddy of mine who was just 24 years old." Steve calls it the toughest call he ever made.

Both parents asked one question each. His father asked, "What's software?" His mother asked, "Why does anybody need a computer?" Steve says neither was a stupid question in 1980, when computers filled rooms. __The people who love you can be wrong about the future and still be right to ask.__

base salary, plus 10% of the profit growth he brought
shares of Microsoft stock he got at first

blocks.text: He arrived on 11 June 1980 as about the 30th employee, with no shares at all. The deal instead gave him a slice of the profit growth he produced, and it would soon become a huge stake in the company. That story belongs to a later chapter. His first workspace, according to Maxwell's biography, was the couch in Gates's office. His first home in Seattle was Bill's place, because he was living with him.

What he found was a chaotic group of brilliant programmers and very little else. "When we got up to 30 [employees], it was still just me, a secretary, and 28 programmers," Gates later recalled. "I wrote all the checks, answered the mail, took the phone calls." Customer lists and invoices were scattered everywhere, and the accounts sat in messy ledgers. Most of the staff reported directly to Gates.
Three days of silence

Within weeks Steve had talked to everyone and reached a conclusion. There was more work than they could honor for their customers, so he went to Gates and said they needed 18 more people. For a company of 30 that was a massive jump. Gates had a very direct answer.
Steve, I didn't ask you to drop out to bankrupt this company.
blocks.who: Bill Gates, as Steve Ballmer remembers it

blocks.text: They were living under the same roof, and they did not speak for ==three days==. When they finally talked, Gates set a test: "Prove to me you can hire one good person and then we'll worry about the other 17." Around the same time Steve hit bottom. He looked at his life and saw that he had thrown away Stanford to be the bookkeeper of a tiny company. He told Gates he was going back.
Best friends. Same house. Three days of silence. Working with friends is hard.

Gates reached for his secret weapon again and brought his father along to dinner, at a place called The Butcher in Bellevue. Steve went through his complaint. Then Gates turned to him and said the sentence that would run Microsoft for nearly two decades. Steve says that he was "mesmerized and afraid of his dad", so he listened.
Steve, Steve, you don't get it, we're going to put a computer on every desk and in every home.
blocks.who: Bill Gates, at dinner in Bellevue, 1980, as Steve Ballmer recalls it

blocks.text: That was not a company slogan yet. It was a 24-year-old trying to stop his friend from quitting. Steve says that recruiting pitch became the company's mantra for the next 17 or 18 years. A few weeks later he bought a house in Seattle. __Sometimes a mission statement is simply what you say when your best person is about to leave.__

The glamour was still a long way off. When the company moved to new offices about a mile away, nobody remembered to file a change of address, and the checks stopped coming. So Steve became the mailman. Every day he drove to the old office, loaded the piled-up mail into the trunk of his car, and delivered it. The Harvard graduate with two Stanford prizes was hauling envelopes.

For example: on 21 September 1980, a large display ad ran in The Seattle Times seeking outstanding programmers. It promised mountains, ocean, desert, rain forest, rivers and lakes all within easy reach. Applications were to go to "Mr. Steve Ballmer, Assistant to the President." He had started on his one good person.

He never went back to Stanford. Years later he told Harvard students that the risk had been smaller than it looked, because good schools let you return, and that he could still finish his MBA to this day. But listen to the other half of his advice. If your kid has a truly compelling idea, he said, hand over some money and tell them to drop out. In the other 99.9999999 percent of cases, tell them to get back to work.

items.text: Enters Harvard planning a PhD. Scores 33 on his first physics exam.
Meets Bill Gates at Currier House. Ranks 57th in the nation on the Putnam.
Graduates magna cum laude and joins Procter & Gamble in Cincinnati.
Tries Hollywood. Reads scripts and parks cars.
Starts at Stanford business school and later wins two $10,000 prizes.
Gates calls: "too bad you don't have a twin brother."
Joins Microsoft. Weeks later, nearly quits, then stays and buys a house.

blocks.text: So that is where the real story starts: a 24-year-old in a house he had just bought, in a city he had first seen a year before. He knew a lot about business, not much about computers, and he had no shares yet. His parents were baffled, and his best friend had just fought him for three days. What he did have was a question to answer: could he hire one good person? He got to work.

factCheck.method: Written from Ballmer's own recorded words wherever possible (Economic Club of Washington 2019, Harvard CS50 2014, Stanford GSB 2007 and 2008, Tools and Weapons 2025, NPR 2019, 60 Minutes 2024/25), then established press (Seattle Times, Harvard Crimson, Harvard Gazette, AP, Fortune, Forbes) and institutional records (Lawrence Tech via CBS Detroit, MAA Michigan Section, Detroit Historical Society, HistoryLink). Limits: the New York Times (Lohr 2007) and Washington Post (Leibovich 2000) passages were read only as excerpts returned by a search tool, because reading the full copies was not permitted, so a fact-checker with access should confirm those quotes against the originals. The Fredric Maxwell biography Bad Boy Ballmer was not read directly; it is used only through the AP report, the manager magazin review (translated from German and paraphrased) and a Summaries.com summary that quotes it. The same summary contains at least one error (it appears to place Scott McNealy at Country Day), so its classmate and teacher quotes are attributed to their speakers and should be checked against the book. Photos and licences come from the Wikimedia Commons API. Nothing here comes from Reddit, Quora or fan pages.

disputed.note: Many sources say a perfect 800 (New York Times, Business Week intro, EBSCO), and The Harvard Crimson says 1600 overall. Ballmer himself said in 2019: "Seven-ninety, not 800." We use his own correction.

disputed.claim: His pay and stake on joining Microsoft
disputed.note: Forbes (Anders 2014): about $50,000 plus 10% of the profit growth he generated, with no shares at first, later swapped for about 8%. Harvard Crimson 2002: $50,000 and 7%. Business Week 2003: $50,000 and some percentage. Ballmer on 60 Minutes: $40,000 and a 9% stake. Business Insider on Gates's memoir says Gates gave up 4% of Microsoft to recruit him. We use Forbes, the most detailed account, and leave the stake to a later chapter.

No. 24 (Business Week intro, USA Today citing Microsoft, Network World), No. 28 (manager magazin on Maxwell), No. 30 (Bloomberg, Forbes, Business Insider, NBA.com). Ballmer consistently says the company had about 30 people. We say "about the 30th".

Ballmer, the Seattle Times and the Washington Post place it in sophomore year at Currier House, about 1974. Business Week's 2003 intro says freshman dorm mates. Business Insider's summary of Gates's memoir says fall 1976, which does not fit Gates leaving Harvard in 1975. A Stanford GSB article calls them roommates, but others say down the hall. We use sophomore year, down the hall.

disputed.claim: Name of the economics class they took together
disputed.note: Crimson: Economics 250. Isaacson in the Harvard Gazette: Economics 2010, taught by Michael Spence. We just say a graduate economics class. Isaacson also credits this class as where they met, while the Washington Post credits an introduction by Jeff Clark.

disputed.claim: Top score on his first Harvard physics exam
disputed.note: In 2014 (CS50) Ballmer said the best score was 75; in 2019 (Economic Club) he said 88 or 90, by Bill Gates's roommate. Both agree he scored 33. We avoid the number.

disputed.claim: Timing of the near-quit and the dinner with Gates's father
disputed.note: Ballmer's retellings vary: two or three weeks in (Tools and Weapons), a month (NPR, CS50), six weeks (Stanford 2005, 2007). The number of extra staff also varies: 18 in Ballmer's versions, 17 in Business Week. We say "within weeks" and use 18.

disputed.claim: When Gates called him at Stanford
disputed.note: 60 Minutes says midway through his first year. Ballmer's 2007 account places it during spring-break job planning in 1980. The Crimson places it in the summer. We use Ballmer's own account.

Described as a mid-level manager (NYT, 60 Minutes), an accountant (Washington Post) and an executive (Seattle Times, NBA.com). Business Week's intro says he dropped out of university in Switzerland; Ballmer said in 2019 that he did not finish high school. We use mid-level and Ballmer's own words.

Business Week: cobbler in Russia. Detroit Jewish News: from Belarus. Seattle Times: calls Ballmer's mother Russian, though Business Week and others say she was born in Detroit. We say Russia, in what is now Belarus, with Detroit as her birthplace.

Business Week's intro and Encyclopedia.com say he played football at Country Day, and a Bad Boy Ballmer summary agrees. Ballmer's own framing in 2019 was that he was not an athlete and was a team manager. We leave football out of the high school story.

"Business manager" in most profiles (Forbes, Crimson, EBSCO); "assistant to the president" in the 1980 Seattle Times ad, and the LA Times timeline of Microsoft. We use the 1980 ad wording where it appears.

disputed.claim: When Gates left Harvard, and how long Ballmer put off Stanford
disputed.note: Business Week says Gates left in his junior year, while other sources have him leaving after sophomore year in 1975. The Crimson says Ballmer deferred Stanford for one year for P&G, while most sources say about two years at P&G (1977 to 1979), including the Hollywood months. We use 1975 and 1977–79.
